prize_parts.citation: For incorporating firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, and showing how the gains from trade operate through reallocation across firms.

statement.case_for: The heterogeneous-firm trade framework is a discrete conceptual advance. Melitz (2003) turned selection into exporting into a dynamic general-equilibrium mechanism, and Helpman's parallel work, including Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple on exports versus FDI, widened it to organisation and multinational activity. It changed what gains from trade mean (reallocation toward more productive firms, not only specialisation across sectors) and tied trade theory to firm-level microdata. Its influence reaches beyond trade into productivity measurement, misallocation and macro models with firm heterogeneity. It is over twenty years old, so its predictions have been tested and extended extensively. It is also a coherent two-person credit, which keeps the citation sharp.
statement.case_against: The credited set leaves out co-originators of the firm-level trade literature (Bernard, Eaton, Jensen, Kortum), so a Helpman-Melitz award could be seen as a contestable cut of a broader programme. Helpman's most distinctive earlier work is arguably closer to the new trade theory that Krugman's 2008 prize recognised, so his marginal credit here needs to be argued on the firm-heterogeneity papers specifically. The size of the welfare gains from trade also still depends on distributional and elasticity assumptions. Separately, B040 has a cleaner and more broadly shared claim: a compact originating paper, a two-person attribution, and strong cross-committee support in the openings. My own rank 1 is not the consensus view, and my closeness to firm-dynamics and reallocation research could bias my weighting.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B040 first because the Kiyotaki-Moore collateral-constraint model is cleanly attributable to two originators and is mature. He ranks B036 last, citing Krugman's 2008 prize and overlap with other trade ballots that split the field's credit.
responses.response: I accept the case for B040: the attribution is cleaner than in most candidates, and I now treat it as my main alternative. On B036, I disagree that Krugman's prize covers the same ground. That prize rewarded increasing returns and product differentiation with representative firms, whereas Melitz introduced within-industry selection and reallocation, which is a different mechanism with different empirical implications. The other trade ballots he mentions, B001 and B043, are not on the shortlist, so on this shortlist they do not compete for credit with B036.

responses.point: Teorell proposes Melitz, Helpman and Redding for B036. He sees Redding's quantitative spatial and trade work as an extension, and he asks whether Helpman or Redding is the better second name.
responses.response: I would stay with Melitz and Helpman. Helpman's contribution is a foundational part of the heterogeneous-firm programme itself (exports versus FDI, firm organisation). Redding's most influential work builds on the framework and on quantitative trade models, and it is better judged as a later strand that may stand on its own. Adding a third name would also dilute a citation that is currently sharp. I agree that the second-name question is real, and I have listed it as an uncertainty.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B036 seventh. He credits Melitz (2003) as the central paper and Helpman for the wider framework, but he notes that Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum contributed to the early firm-level evidence and are not credited, and that overlap with other trade candidates complicates attribution.
responses.response: I agree on attribution, and I am not claiming the credited list is complete. The omission of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum is the strongest reservation against B036. I read it as a limit on how much can be credited under a three-name cap, not as a reason to withhold credit from the theory that explained why those empirical facts arise. Where I differ from Andersson is the weighting. The explanatory model plus the gains-from-trade reallocation result seems to me a larger contribution than the earlier descriptive exporter-premium evidence, which the model rationalised.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B002 first because population-scale administrative data changed how mobility and neighbourhood effects are measured. He is cautious about maturity and about crediting a large team.
responses.response: I share his regard for the programme and kept it as an alternative. My reservation is timing and attribution. The core results are about a decade old, the causal interpretation of place effects is still being tested, and credit is spread across many collaborators. With the two-person or three-person limit, that makes it harder to define a stable citation now than for the heterogeneous-firm framework, whose predictions have been tested for two decades.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee would treat Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum as co-originators who should be credited alongside or instead of Helpman.
Whether Helpman's marginal credit here is distinct enough from the new trade theory recognised in 2008.
Whether B040's cleaner attribution and broader support should outweigh B036 once the overlap with the 2022 financial-crisis prize is weighed.
How robust the quantitative welfare gains from firm heterogeneity are to distributional and elasticity assumptions.
My assessments rely on general knowledge from the supplied openings and profile; I have not independently verified citations or impact.
statement.conflict_note: Klenow is a long-standing co-author of mine, but he is credited only on B006, which I am not proposing. I also co-author with the secretary Per Krusell and the chair John Hassler and am a colleague of both at IIES, and I co-authored with Aghion, Bergeaud, Klenow and Li on creative-destruction growth measurement; none of these people is credited on B036. My research on firm dynamics and reallocation is thematically close to B036. These are disclosed, not adjudicated.
